sets.title: Football Tournament - Points and Goals
sets.context:
A football tournament was played between three teams, A, B and C, with each pair playing one match. Scoring rules: (i) a team gets 2 points for every goal it scores against the opponent; (ii) a team gets 1 extra point for every one of those goals scored from outside the 'D' area; (iii) a team loses 1 point for every goal it concedes. Only three players from each team scored goals across the tournament.
Match A vs B: B won this match and got 4 points from it. Team A scored two goals in this match. No player scored a goal from outside the D area in this match.
Match A vs C: C got zero points from this match. Only one player from team A scored a goal from outside the D area in this match. A secured four points from this match.
Match B vs C: B got six points from this match, and team C scored one goal more than B did in it. Only one player from team B scored a goal from outside the D area in this match.

Working the scoring rules through each match gives: A scored 2 goals and conceded 3 in the A-B match (net 4 - 3 = 1 point), then scored 2 and conceded 1 (with a bonus) in the A-C match (4 points) - so A totals 4 goals and 5 points. B scored 3 goals (2x2+... with the concession penalty) for 4 points in the A-B match, then scored 6 goals for 6 points in the B-C match - so B totals 9 goals and 10 points. C scored 1 goal (0 points, after conceding) in the A-C match, then scored 7 goals for 8 points in the B-C match - so C totals 8 goals and 8 points.

sets.title: RC: Deforestation and Global Warming
sets.context:
Global warming, largely caused by industrial development and consumer demands, has been causing havoc across the world. Temperatures are shooting up, floods have been ravaging South China and Northeast India, and unseasonal rains and, ironically, delayed and poor monsoon rains are experienced. A major solution to **mitigate** such climate changes is to reduce the levels of greenhouse gases, particularly carbon dioxide, which causes this warming. In an effort to limit this warming, many countries across the world are gathering together and agreeing to make efforts to limit the rise in temperature to no higher than 1.5 degrees by the year 2050. The major way to do so is to increase the number of plants, trees and forests across the world. They all absorb carbon dioxide from the air, and with the help of sunlight and water, produce food (staple for us) and oxygen (which we breathe). And the wood and timber they offer are used by us in buildings and furniture. They are, thus, justly named in Sanskrit as Kalpataru - the wish-giving tree.

Yet, we kill them: deforestation has been going on decade after decade across the world, affecting the weather as well as the lives of plants, animals, microbes and the livelihood of human tribes that live in forests. The total surface area of our Earth is 52 billion hectares, and 31% of this has been forest cover. But the huge Amazon forests of South America are being chopped down for commercial reasons. Peru and Bolivia in the western Amazon region are the worst affected by such deforestation; so are Mexico and its neighbours in Mesoamerica. Russia, with forests occupying 45% of its land area, is also chopping down trees. Large-scale deforestation of this kind has contributed to global warming over the years.

The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) defines a 'forest' as a land area of at least 0.5 hectares, covered by at least 10% tree cover, ______________________________. Using this definition, a group of Swiss and French ecologists have analysed the 4.4 billion hectares of tree canopy that can exist under the current climate. Excluding existing trees and agricultural and urban areas, there is room for an extra 0.9 billion hectares. Their analysis, using the latest ecological methods, was published two weeks ago - showing the potential for climate change mitigation through global tree restoration. They point out that more than 50% of this restoration potential can be found in just six countries (Russia, USA, Canada, Australia, Brazil and China). While it is not clear how much of this land is public or private, they confirm that a total of 1 billion hectares (with over 10% tree cover) is achievable.

Happily enough, several groups (and governments) in countries, notably the Philippines and State governments in India, have moved towards more tree plantations. In India, with its 7,08,273 sq km land area, 21.54% has tree cover, and between 2015 and 2018 India added 6,778 sq km of tree cover. Madhya Pradesh has the largest forest cover, followed by Chhattisgarh, Odisha and Arunachal Pradesh, while Punjab, Haryana, UP and Rajasthan have the least.

sets.title: Cloze: Reviving the Iran Nuclear Deal (JCPOA)
sets.context:

This game of chicken continues as the clock is ticking. Iran will elect a new President in June. Hassan Rouhani, who bet his presidency on the deal - only to be repudiated by Mr. Trump - cannot stand in a third consecutive election. There is no guarantee that a moderate like Mr. Rouhani would be elected this time, and it is not a secret that there is considerable opposition among the hardliners, a powerful constituency, towards any kind of ___(90)___ with the U.S. Mr. Biden's best bet is to get the nuclear agreement back on track before Mr. Rouhani leaves office.

To be sure, Mr. Biden has moved with a sense of urgency after ___(91)___ power. He appointed a special envoy for Iran, showed signs of rebalancing ties with Saudi Arabia, and sent clear signals to Tehran about America's desire to get back to the deal. But these actions do not seem to be enough to ___(92)___ the trust after the acrimonious Trump years. Some of Iran's concerns are genuine. After the September 11, 2001 terrorist attack, Iran had cooperated with the U.S. in the war against the Taliban. But once the Taliban were ___(93)___ out of power, the Bush administration branded Iran as part of an 'Axis of Evil' along with Iraq and North Korea. As President Barack Obama offered diplomacy, the Iranians grabbed the opportunity, leading to the signing of the JCPOA in 2015.

sets.title: RC: UAE Tourism, MICE Industry and COVID-19
sets.context:
The development of the MICE industry (meetings, incentives, conferences and events) contributes to economic diversification, stimulates the rational use of cultural and natural-recreational resources, and enables a balanced growth of the whole tourism sector. For the United Arab Emirates (UAE), the tourism sector is especially important as a driver of national gross domestic product (GDP). As stated by the Dubai Annual Visitor Report 2019, at the end of 2019, tourism was **responsible** for contributing an impressive 11.5 per cent of GDP value. Furthermore, according to the World Travel and Tourism Council's Cities Report, Dubai's tourism sector was ranked one of the 'Top 10' strongest economic-share generators.

More than 2.3 million visitors cited business as their main purpose of travel to Dubai in 2019, marking a two per cent increase compared to 2018. In 2019, Dubai World Trade Centre (DWTC) welcomed a record 3.57 million delegates, which **declared** the visitation growth of up to four per cent from the previous year. Such an increase was driven by 349 MICE and business events, 97 of which were large-scale with over 2,000 attendees. Since 2019, international participation in DWTC events grew by 15 per cent (equivalent to 1.2 million visitors), underlining the strong benefits world businesses see in coming to Dubai to share knowledge, network and accelerate their development. Last year, business tourism events accounted for 3.3% of GDP, amounting to USD 3.57 billion. Business tourism was a key element in **stimulating** national economic growth, and in the near future was supposed to reach intense development, making the UAE among the central players in the global MICE industry. However, the introduced quarantine ruined these plans.

The COVID-19 pandemic has led to more than 4.3 million confirmed cases and more than 290,000 deaths worldwide. It raised fears of an impending economic crisis and recession. Social distancing, self-isolation, and travel restrictions have **reduced** the workforce in all sectors of the economy and have led to the loss of many jobs. Due to the lack of a vaccine and very limited treatment options, non-pharmaceutical interventions occurred to be the primary strategy to contain the pandemic. Unprecedented global travel restrictions and appeals to stay at home have caused the most critical disruptions of the global economy since World War II. Given the international travel bans that effect more than 90% of the global population and widespread restrictions on public gatherings and community mobility, tourism largely ceased in March 2020. Since the quarantine's introduction, millions of jobs in the global tourism sector were lost due to flight, event and hotel cancellations.

Given that international arrivals exceeded 1.5 billion for the first time only in 2019, the long-term evolution of tourism is proved to be **great** dependent on a decade of growth since the global financial crisis. Though, this last period of unhindered business tourism development has suddenly come to an end with COVID-19.

Accompanied by quarantine in most countries and closed borders worldwide, the COVID-19 pandemic heavily hit the MICE industry. The majority of domestic and international airlines were forced to cancel their flights due ________________________, as people were frightened. The MICE industry was undermined by government efforts to contain and combat the pandemic. Borders were closed, trips banned, social and business events cancelled, and people were ordered to stay in their homes. By taking these actions, governments around the world sought to strike a balance between maintaining their economies and preventing dangerous levels of unemployment and deprivation.

questions.question:
In the question below are given two conclusions followed by some sets of statements. Choose the set of statements that logically satisfies both conclusions given, even if the statements seem to be at variance with commonly known facts.
Conclusions: I. All Home can be Office. II. Some Party is not Building.
options: No Office is Home. No Office is Building. All Office is Party.
No Home is Building. All Office is Home. All Party is Building.
All Home is Party. All Office is Party. No Office is Building.
All Building is Home. Some Home is Office. Some Office is Party.

questions.question:
A can complete a piece of work in 'a' days by working 'm' hours per day, and B can complete the same work in 'b' days by working 'n' hours per day. If each of them reduces their working hours per day by 4 hours, each of them would take 5 days more to finish the work (m, n < 16, and m, n, a, b are all integers). Which of the following is/are possible values for the time taken if A and B work together, with A working 'm' hours per day and B working 'n' hours per day?
I. 5 days
II. 4 days
III. 10/3 days
IV. 2.5 days
V. 3 1/2 days
questions.explanation: From a x m = (a+5)(m-4), we get 5m - 4a = 20, whose integer solutions with m < 16 are (m,a) = (8,5) or (12,10); the same equation and constraint give (n,b) = (8,5) or (12,10) for B. Combined work rate (in days) = ab/(a+b): for a=5,b=5 -> 2.5 days; for a=5,b=10 (or a=10,b=5) -> 50/15 = 10/3 days; for a=10,b=10 -> 5 days. So the achievable times are 2.5, 10/3 and 5 days - matching I, III and IV.

questions.question:
Compare the following three quantities.
Quantity I: India's chances of winning a match against England are 1/5. What is the minimum number of matches India should play against England so that there is a fair (at least 50%) chance of winning at least one match?
Quantity II: How many five-digit numbers are possible where the unit digit is prime, and the product of all the digits of that number is also prime?
Quantity III: A and B start walking towards each other at 6 AM at respective speeds of 5 km/h and 8 km/h. They meet at a point, stop for coffee, and at 12:04 PM resume walking towards their original destinations. Find the time spent on coffee (in minutes), if A reaches his destination at 9:40 PM.
options: Quantity II < Quantity I <= Quantity III
Quantity I < Quantity III <= Quantity II
Quantity III = Quantity II > Quantity III
Quantity II >= Quantity III = Quantity I
questions.explanation: Quantity I: need 1-(4/5)^x >= 1/2, i.e. (4/5)^x <= 1/2; testing x=4 gives 256/625 < 1/2 (the first x that works), so minimum matches = 4. Quantity II: for the digit product to be prime, four of the five digits must be 1 and the fifth (the prime unit digit) supplies the only prime factor, giving numbers 11112, 11113, 11115, 11117 - so 4 such numbers. Quantity III: if they meet t hours after 6 AM, B has then covered 8t km, which A must cover afterward at 5 km/h to reach the original meeting-adjacent destination by 9:40 PM; solving the timeline gives t = 6 hours (meeting at noon), and the coffee break lasts from 12:00 PM to 12:04 PM, i.e. 4 minutes. All three quantities equal 4, but since none of the listed strict-inequality patterns captures 'all three equal', the answer is 'None of these'.
